## **Impact Assessment (IA) of Wind Energy Projects utilizing Environment Canada (EC) guidelines**

Reg. B. Ejeckam[1] , M.Sc., P. Geo., & Paul E. Gregoire[2] , M.Sc. Charles M. Francis, PhD[3] .

## ABSTRACT

Wind power projects can adversely affect birds and bats through collisions or interactions with blades and habitat degradation. With the rapid expansion of the wind energy sector in Canada, it has become necessary to ensure that adverse environmental effects are understood and mitigated or managed.  An EC guidance document was developed for EA practitioners to facilitate their review of wind project Environmental Impact Assessments (EIA) before projects are started.  This guideline, entitled “ _Wind Turbines and Birds: A Guidance Document for Environmental Assessment_ “, includes consideration of impacts on Migratory Birds and Species at Risk, with further consideration of wetlands and bats during site selection, project design, collection of baseline data, and post-construction monitoring. It also outlines factors to consider and information that should be collected and analyzed for inclusion in an EIA. The presentation will describe this guideline and provide practical examples of our experiences with wind energy projects.

Keywords: Wind Energy, Birds, Bats, Species at Risk, Migratory Birds, Environment Canada, Environmental Assessment, CanWEA, Canada.

## Introduction

Environment Canada (EC) recognizes the benefit of Wind Energy and the rapid increase in Wind Energy projects across the country.  Wind turbines are strategically situated in areas where there is consistent wind to be able to power or turn the turbines. These areas are typically ridges, elevated areas, and in some cases open fields with few obstructions. Unfortunately, these areas are also good corridors for migration or habitat for birds and other wild life. A guideline was developed to help industry design and implement wind energy projects to minimize the impact on wildlife, and in particular migratory birds and species that are listed or covered under the Species at Risk Act. It is also meant to guide EC environmental assessment (EA) practitioners and permitting agencies.

## Rapid growth of Wind Energy in Canada

In the last seven years the installed capacity of Wind Energy in Canada has grown from 236 MW to about 2369 MW, (Table 1). Close to 3,000 MW of signed power purchase agreements are in place and to be constructed within the next few years, and approximately 3,300 MW of additional power purchase agreements were signed in 2008 (Table 1). The Canadian Wind Energy Association (CanWEA) projected that by 2016, there would be 12,000 MW of wind energy installed capacity in Canada.  The association argues in their Wind Vision 2025 document that by year 2025, 20% of Canada’s energy supply should come from Wind energy. This will bring the total capacity Wind energy projects to about 55,000 MW. (CanWEA).

With the rapid expansion of the wind energy sector, it has become necessary to ensure that adverse environmental effects are understood and mitigated or consistently managed appropriately and consistently across the country. Wind power projects can adversely affect wildlife, including birds or bats through direct collisions with blades and or habitat degradation due to noise, avoidance or interference on migration pathways and destruction of habitats such as native grassland, forests and wetlands.

## Guidelines to Environmental Assessment for Wind Energy Projects

Environment Canada’s legislative mandate includes being responsible for the Migratory Birds Convention Act (MBCA), Species at Risk Act (SARA), and implementation of the government policy on Wetland conservation.

Environmental Assessment of Wind Energy Projects in Canada is required to take into

consideration its impact on wildlife especially Migratory Birds and Species at Risk, as well as considerations for wetlands and bats during site selection, project design, collection of baseline data, and post construction monitoring.

_Wind Turbines and Birds: A Guidance Document for Environmental Assessment_ (hereafter referred to as ‘the guide’) was developed by EC in consultation with industry, CanWEA, different levels of government and EA practitioners and is based on studies done by Bird Studies Canada Andrea Kingsley and Becky Whittam (2005) under contract to Environment Canada. The guide specifies steps which are intended to enhance information gathering by the industry and guide them in compilation of pre-construction baseline data that would aid a thorough preparation of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). (A second document entitled _Recommended Protocols for Monitoring Impacts of Wind Turbines on Birds (Environment Canada 2006) is also available_ , however only the first is considered in this paper.)

The objectives of the guide were:

(i) To help or guide industries or proponents proposing to develop Wind Energy projects in making the best choices with regard to the location of wind farms;

(ii) To help or guide the regulatory agencies that issue approvals or authorization for the projects to determine the completeness and thoroughness of information provided by the proponent, and to ensure that all necessary factors were considered before making a permitting decisions.  In addition, it also guides EC EA practitioners in their review of the Environmental Impact Assessment.

(iii) Most importantly, to identify the amount and type of baseline information that the proponent needs to collect from field surveys prior to preparing their EIA. It also suggests the most appropriate times of the year when such surveys are most effective. This will in general help to reduce the amount of time it will take to complete EIA and its review.

The guide is divided into 8 steps to guide the proponent on how to go from the initial data review (step1) to the verification of predictions and effectiveness of mitigation measures (step 8). Below are brief summaries of the steps. These steps are explained in more details in the guidance document.  As stated in the guide, _“This Guide is intended for educational purposes only. It should not be perceived as a substitute for the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, the Species at Risk Act or any other federal legislation referred to in this Guide. In the event of any inconsistency between this Guide and the legislation, the latter would prevail. Individuals with specific legal problems are urged to seek legal advice”. (EC, 2006)_

The sections in the guide related to the steps are included in brackets for clarity.

- Step 1: Pre-assessment considerations (Section 3). This initial step encourages the industry to verify first through preliminary literature search or contacting the appropriate agencies whether the intended area or location of their proposed wind farm contains any or nearby bird or wildlife area that is considered important or sensitive, or an area designated as sensitive to disturbance.

- Step 2: Preliminary information required (Section 4). Compile any available data published and unpublished or search any existing database, including even traditional knowledge of those who live in the area. This step may well include a reconnaissance field survey, to determine the bird populations and habitats that may be affected by the proposed wind farm. In some cases, knowledge of the affected geographic area can be used to search several registries or databases to determine what bird species are likely to exist in the area, their use of the area and what time of year and the type of survey that is likely to be required.  For example Environment Canada’s guide to Canada’s species at risk in the Prairie Provinces listed several species at risk in the Prairie with maps showing the range where these species are likely to exist. This step will also help the proponent determine data gaps and how rigorous and extensive its subsequent survey must be.

- Step 3: Determination of site sensitivity (Section 5). Information collected from steps 1 & 2 will help the proponent to determine how environmentally sensitive the proposed area is. Table 1 in the guidance document utilized these factors to rank sensitivity of sites.

- Step 4: Size of the facility (Section 6). The proposed size of the wind farm will in a way determine the severity of the cumulative effect of the turbines in the area. Table 2 in the guidance document used the cumulative number of turbines to determine the project’s size ranking. For example an area that contains one to 10 turbines may be considered low in the category ranking, whereas if the same area was to contain 100 turbines or more, it will be considered very high in the ranking.

- Step 5: Determining the project level of concern category (Section 7). Using a matrix based on site sensitivity (step 3) and facility size (step 4) the proponent can classify the project into categories, with the over riding issue being how sensitive the site is. When sensitivity is taken together with size, the level of concern is determined.  For example if an area is considered very sensitive, and the proponent plans a very large number of turbines in the area, it becomes obvious that the level of concern will be high. The higher level of concern will imply a more detailed data collection and analysis of data to determine potential impact on birds, in particular, as well as suitability of the site.

- Step 6: Determining the level of baseline information needed (Section 8). Once the above steps have been completed, the results will guide the proponent in determining how rigorous or how detailed the baseline data need to be, in order to adequately characterize the site. Regardless of the level of concern, proponents are always encouraged to consult Environment Canada whenever in doubt.

- Step 7: General considerations relating to facility or site design (Section 9). The answers to the baseline information questions can assist in determining the potential environmental effects of the proposed project, and can be applied directly to modify the design and layout of the wind energy installation of the turbines to reduce impacts on birds.

- Step 8: Verify predictions and mitigation effectiveness (Section 10). The project level of concern category may be adjusted following the analysis of baseline information, and will then guide the

extent of follow-up that is needed to determine actual environmental effects of the project. In some cases, this information may suggest mitigation measures beyond the initially proposed ones. It will also contribute to cumulative impact assessment that may influence future projects.

## Some monitoring results of Wind Farms

The Government of Canada has reviewed several hundred wind farms over the past few years. A number of post mortality monitoring reports have been submitted but there are still a number that have yet to be completed.  Thus far, most wind farms have been showing low levels of bird and bat mortality, and avoidance by birds.  However we do have several instances where high bat mortality was observed. In one case, two wind farms have picked up an average of 10 bats per turbine per year, observer bias and scavenger removal would probably make the actual number higher.  It should be noted that both of these wind farms are located in agricultural lands.  Five hundred (500) bats were picked up over one year at one farm with 38 turbines (Ottawa Citizen, 2008) and more than 350 bats were picked up over a year at another farm with 35 turbines (CBC 2008). Most of the mortality was concentrated during the fall migration period.  Similarly, some raptors are getting killed; up to 4-5 per year for a couple wind farms.  The number is not alarming but does show some vulnerability for raptors.  Bird mortality has been shown to be noticeably reduced with turbines located greater than 150 meters from the great lakes shorelines have been recorded.  These results do show some impact of wind farms on bird and bats; however, it is unclear at this time how closely these proponents followed EC’s guidelines.

## Conclusion

_The Wind Turbines and Birds: A Guidance Document for Environmental Assessment_ outlined 8 steps that suggest the amount and type of data that are needed for a thorough EIA for a Wind Farm in Canada.

The preparation of _the Wind Turbines and Birds: A Guidance Document for Environmental Assessment_ was an effort to bring together the concerns of Environment Canada regarding the protection of wildlife with inputs from the Industry and other levels of government to reduce the time it takes to review an EIA.  If the industry complies with the suggested steps outlined in the guidance document, it would collect, compile and integrate the required information into its EIA, which the regulators would be looking for when evaluating the proposed project. This will in effect reduce the turn around time for the review and evaluation of projects. It will also eliminate the usual regulator’s request for more information or more surveys. It also shows that the industry and the regulators can work collaboratively in protecting the environment.

## Recommendations

We recommend that:

(a) Industry acquaints themselves with the guidelines early in the planning process in order to determine what is needed for Environmental Assessment.

(b) Wind Energy Developers are also encouraged to affiliate themselves with the Canadian Wind

Energy Association (CanWEA) and their practices because the companies that are affiliated with CanWEA have experienced fewer  problems with the regulatory requirements and practices than those who are not

(c ),  Wind energy companies are advised to contact the local offices of Environment Canada early in the environmental assessment process for advice regarding the guidelines.
